real-nominal-gdp-s3.title: A headline about record GDP
real-nominal-gdp-s3.text: A news site in Country Q reports: "GDP hits a record! Nominal GDP rose 6% this year, the biggest jump in a decade." Further down, the article notes that the GDP deflator rose 7% over the same year and that the population grew 1%.

items.q: What is nominal GDP in Year 2, in dollars?

why.correct: Nominal GDP uses each year's own prices: $120 \times 2.50 + 50 \times 5 = 300 + 250 = 550$ dollars.

mistakes.why: That uses Year 1 prices, which gives real GDP. Nominal GDP values Year 2 output at Year 2 prices.

items.q: What is real GDP in Year 2, measured in Year 1 prices, in dollars?

why.correct: Real GDP values this year's quantities at base-year prices: $120 \times 2 + 50 \times 4 = 240 + 200 = 440$ dollars.

mistakes.why: That is nominal GDP, at Year 2 prices. Real GDP keeps prices at the base year so only quantities change.
That uses Year 1 quantities as well as Year 1 prices: it is Year 1 GDP. Use Year 2 quantities.

items.q: What is the GDP deflator in Year 2?

why.correct: Deflator $= \frac{\text{nominal GDP}}{\text{real GDP}} \times 100 = \frac{550}{440} \times 100 = 125$. Prices of the goods in GDP are 25% above the base year.

mistakes.why: The fraction is upside down: you divided real by nominal. The deflator is nominal over real, times 100, and it is above 100 when prices have risen.
You divided but did not multiply by 100. The deflator is an index, with the base year at 100.

items.q: By what percent did real GDP grow from Year 1 to Year 2?

why.correct: Real GDP was $400$ in Year 1 (the base year, so real equals nominal) and $440$ in Year 2: $\frac{440 - 400}{400} \times 100 = 10\%$.

mistakes.why: That is the growth of nominal GDP, which includes the price rise. Compare real GDP in the two years to see how much output grew.

items.q: What is Halvet's real GDP in Year 2, in billions of dollars?

mistakes.why: You multiplied by the deflator. Prices rose, so to remove the price rise divide by the deflator, then multiply by 100.
You divided by the deflator but did not multiply by 100. The deflator is an index on a base of 100.

items.q: Did Halvet's output of goods and services grow from Year 1 to Year 2?
options: No: real GDP fell from 800 to 750
Yes: nominal GDP rose from 800 to 900
Yes: the deflator rose from 100 to 120
The data are not enough to say

why.correct: To judge whether output grew, compare real GDP. Nominal GDP can rise with no growth at all if prices rise enough.
options: Right: nominal GDP rose only because prices rose 20%; output itself fell.
Nominal GDP mixes output and prices; here the whole rise, and more, is higher prices.
A rising deflator shows prices went up, not output.
Nominal GDP and the deflator are all you need: divide to get real GDP.

items.q: What is the growth rate of Halvet's real GDP from Year 2 to Year 3?

why.correct: Real GDP in Year 3 is $\frac{990}{110} \times 100 = 900$. Growth $= \frac{900 - 750}{750} \times 100 = 20\%$.

mistakes.why: That is nominal GDP growth. Convert each year to real GDP first (750 and 900), then find the percent change.

items.q: What happened to prices of the goods in Halvet's GDP from Year 2 to Year 3?
options: They stayed the same, because both years are after the base year
They fell on average, because the deflator fell from 120 to 110
They rose, because nominal GDP rose
They rose 10%, the change in nominal GDP

why.correct: The GDP deflator is a price index for everything in GDP, so its percent change measures inflation or, here, deflation.
options: Being after the base year says nothing about the change between two later years.
Right: a falling deflator is deflation for the goods in GDP, about 8.3%.
Nominal GDP rose because real output rose a lot; the deflator, the price measure, fell.
The change in nominal GDP mixes prices and output; the deflator shows prices fell.

items.q: Based on the full article, what happened to Country Q's real GDP this year?
options: It rose by about 13%
It rose by about 5%, after population growth
It fell by about 1%
It rose by about 6%, a record

why.correct: Nominal GDP growth is about real growth plus inflation, so real growth is about nominal growth minus the change in the deflator.
options: A rising deflator is subtracted from nominal growth, not added.
Population growth matters for output per person, but the first step is removing price changes.
Right: real growth is about nominal growth minus the rise in the deflator: $6 - 7 = -1\%$.
Six percent is the nominal rise, which includes higher prices.

items.q: Which measure would best show whether the typical living standard in Country Q rose this year?
options: Nominal GDP
The GDP deflator
Nominal GDP per capita
Real GDP per capita

why.correct: Real GDP per capita adjusts for both prices and population. Here real GDP fell about 1% and the population grew 1%, so it fell about 2%.
options: Nominal GDP includes the 7% rise in prices and ignores population.
The deflator is a price index; it says nothing about output per person.
Dividing by population helps, but nominal figures still include the rise in prices.
Right: it removes price changes and divides by population, giving output per person.
The rise in nominal GDP came from higher prices, not more output
Nominal GDP leaves out government purchases
A 6% rise in nominal GDP is too small to be a record
GDP can't rise in a year when population grows

why.correct: Headlines about nominal GDP mix output and prices. Divide by the deflator to see what happened to production.
options: Right: with prices up 7%, the 6% rise in nominal GDP hides a fall in real output.
Nominal GDP includes C, I, G and net exports; the problem is prices.
Whether it is a record in nominal terms is not the issue; nominal GDP is the wrong measure of output.
GDP can rise with population; the issue is that prices rose more than GDP.

items.q: A country's nominal GDP is 600 billion dollars and its real GDP is 500 billion dollars. What is its GDP deflator?

why.correct: $\frac{600}{500} \times 100 = 120$. Prices of the goods in GDP are 20% above the base year.

mistakes.why: The fraction is upside down: real over nominal. The deflator is nominal over real, times 100.
You divided but did not multiply by 100. A deflator is an index, so the base year is 100, not 1.

items.q: In a year before the base year, a country's nominal GDP is 400 billion dollars and its GDP deflator is 80. What is its real GDP, in billions of dollars?

why.correct: $\frac{400}{80} \times 100 = 500$ billion. Prices were lower than in the base year, so real GDP (at base-year prices) is larger than nominal GDP.

mistakes.why: You multiplied by the deflator. Divide by it, then multiply by 100: with a deflator below 100, real GDP comes out above nominal.

items.q: In the base year, how do nominal GDP and real GDP compare?
options: They can't be compared in the base year
They are equal, and the GDP deflator is 100
Nominal GDP is larger, because it uses current prices
Real GDP is larger, because it removes inflation

why.correct: Real GDP uses base-year prices and nominal GDP uses current prices. In the base year these are the same prices, so the deflator is 100.
options: They can: they are equal by definition.
Right: in the base year, current prices are the base-year prices.
In the base year current prices are base-year prices, so the two are the same.
There is nothing to remove in the base year: the prices are the same.

items.q: Why do economists use real GDP rather than nominal GDP to measure changes in output over time?
options: Real GDP is measured in current prices
Real GDP is larger than nominal GDP in each year
Real GDP holds prices fixed, so only quantities move it
Real GDP includes used goods and transfers

why.correct: Valuing every year's output at the same base-year prices means changes in real GDP reflect changes in production.
options: That is nominal GDP; real GDP uses base-year prices.
Real GDP is smaller than nominal after the base year when prices have risen.
Right: nominal GDP can rise from higher prices alone; real GDP removes that.
Real and nominal GDP count the same goods; only the prices used differ.

items.q: How does the GDP deflator differ from the consumer price index?
options: It measures the cost of a fixed basket bought by typical households
It is measured in dollars, not as an index
It includes the prices of imported consumer goods
It prices everything produced in the country, not a basket

why.correct: The deflator is a price index for everything in GDP; the CPI is a price index for a basket of consumer goods and services.
options: That describes the CPI.
Both are indexes with a base year of 100.
Imports are not produced in the country, so they are outside GDP and its deflator; the CPI includes them.
Right: the deflator includes investment and government purchases and leaves out imports; the CPI prices what households buy, imports included.

items.q: Nominal GDP rose last year. Which of these could explain the rise? Select all that apply.
options: Prices fell 4% while output stayed the same
Output rose while prices stayed the same
Prices rose while output stayed the same
Prices rose 5% while output fell 2%
Prices and output both fell
Prices stayed the same while output fell

why.correct: Nominal GDP is output times current prices, so it can rise from more output, higher prices or both. Only real GDP isolates output.
options: Lower prices on the same output mean lower nominal GDP.
Right: more output at the same prices raises nominal GDP.
Right: higher prices on the same output raise nominal GDP.
Right: nominal GDP rises by about $5 - 2 = 3\%$.
If both fell, nominal GDP would fall too.
At constant prices, less output means lower nominal GDP.
